authoredPrompt: This figure shows cyclohexane in its chair form through three labeled panels, (a), (b), and (c). Panel (a) is a ball-and-stick model of the six-membered ring: six dark gray carbon spheres joined by pale rods trace a shape that rises at one end and dips at the other, each carbon carrying two off-white hydrogen spheres. Panel (b) redraws the same ring as a line structure with the near bonds bolded to signal depth, its carbons numbered 1 through 6 in magenta and its hydrogens lettered in magenta, green, blue, and black. Two drawn eyes at the right, marked "Observer", send magenta dashed sightlines to carbon 1 and to carbon 5. Panel (c) is the corresponding Newman projection: two circles, each with a front carbon dot and three bonds, are joined at the top and bottom by groups written "CH2", with the front atoms numbered 1 and 5 and the surrounding hydrogens numbered 2, 3, 4, and 6 in matching colors. Carrying the same numbering and hydrogen colors through all three panels lets the reader map any position on the model onto the corresponding position in the end-on view. Together the panels demonstrate that the chair shape holds its bond angles near the tetrahedral value while keeping every pair of neighboring C-H bonds staggered, leaving the ring free of strain.
authoredInteractions:
- Click for selecting carbon 1 or carbon 5 in the line drawing; the matching front carbon, hydrogens, and CH2 connectors highlight in the Newman projection, clarifying how positions transfer between representations.
- Toggle among ball-and-stick, line structure, and Newman projection panels; the ball-and-stick view establishes the 3D chair shape, while the line structure and Newman projection carry the matching hydrogen colors used to track staggered neighboring C-H bonds.
authoredContext:
Cyclohexane adopts a strain-free, three-dimensional shape that is called a chair conformation because of its similarity to a lounge chair, with a back, seat, and footrest (the figure). Chair cyclohexane has neither angle strain nor torsional strain—all C−C−C bond angles are near the 109° tetrahedral value, and all neighboring C−H bonds are staggered.

The strain-free chair conformation of cyclohexane. All C−C−C bond angles are 111.5°, close to the ideal 109° tetrahedral angle, and all neighboring C−H bonds are staggered.

The ball and stick model, chair conformation, and Newman projection of cyclohexane. The carbon atoms are numbered in chair conformation and Newman projection.

The easiest way to visualize chair cyclohexane is to build a molecular model if you have access to a model kit, or alternatively to explore with one of the many computer-based modeling programs you may have access to.

discrepancies: Panel (a) hydrogens are slightly larger relative to carbons than in the source ball-and-stick rendering, and the bonds lack the subtle two-tone shading of the source
In panel (b) the source shows a clear bold/thin bond weight hierarchy across the whole chair; the generated near/far thickness split (based on z) may not match the source's specific bold edges
Eyes in panel (b) are stylized spheres with cone irises rather than the sketched eye profile icons of the source
Panel (c) numbering placement (2/3 left, 4/6 right, CH2 labels) is approximate and may not match the exact spoke-to-number mapping of the source
evaluation.notes: All three source panels (ball-and-stick chair, line structure with observer sightlines, dual Newman projections) are implemented behind a toggle with a meaningful click-to-highlight linkage between panels; the chair pucker and axial/equatorial H geometry are correct, with only minor proportion and label-mapping differences from the source.

Verify the carbon numbering and H color mapping on the Newman spokes in panel (c) against the source (positions 2,3 vs 4,6 and CH2 label placement)
